items.quote: Then the man who had the evil spirit jumped on them and overpowered them all. He gave them such a beating that they ran out of the house naked and bleeding.
items.contrast: The beaten seven sons run out, not the man who attacked them.
items.reason: The man with the evil spirit is the attacker, while “them” and “they” refer back to the seven sons. Resolving the pronouns distinguishes the attacker from his victims.

items.quote: left that town in search of some other place to stay.
items.contrast: His purpose is finding another place to stay; reaching Micah’s house is a later event, not his stated reason for leaving.
items.reason: The passage directly states the Levite’s purpose for leaving and separately describes what happened on his way.

items.quote: So he said to his sons, “Saddle the donkey for me.” And when they had saddled the donkey for him, he mounted it
items.contrast: The sons saddle the donkey, but their father, the old prophet, mounts it.
items.reason: The change from “they” to “he” distinguishes the sons who prepare the donkey from the old prophet who rides it.

items.quote: Take this young man to the commander; he has something to tell him.
items.contrast: The young man has information for the commander; Paul is the speaker sending him.
items.reason: In Paul’s command, “he” refers to “this young man,” while “him” refers to the commander. The reader must distinguish the messenger from Paul, who gives the instruction.

items.quote: Then they said to him, “Please inquire of God to learn whether our journey will be successful.” The priest answered them
items.contrast: They address the priest and ask him to inquire of God; God is the intended source of the guidance, not the person they address.
items.reason: The priest’s response identifies him as the person addressed. The request distinguishes the intermediary being asked from God, whom he is to inquire of.
